_about: Words and phrases from the comparative questions, explained in plain English. Shown when a student taps one in a question (eng.js qMark). kind: task (what the question tells you to do) or topic (what it's about). match: the forms to find, longest first; eg: an example from each text, where there's a clear one.

terms.def: How far, or how much. Don't just say yes or no: say how much it's true, and where it's more true or less true.
terms.do: Give a judgement of degree: completely, largely, partly, hardly at all, and in which text most.

terms.def: Talk it through, point by point, with evidence. You can agree, disagree, or say it's partly true.
terms.do: Make a clear argument and back every point with a key moment.

terms.def: Show how the texts are alike and how they're different on this point.
terms.do: Bring the texts together inside each paragraph: similarly, in contrast, to a greater extent.

terms.def: Show the differences between the texts.
terms.do: Put the texts side by side and say how they differ, and why it matters.

terms.def: Name it clearly, so the examiner knows exactly what you're writing about.
terms.do: Say what it is in your first sentence.

terms.def: Say why or how, not just what.
terms.do: After each point, add because..., which shows...

terms.def: Build each point out properly with evidence and explanation, rather than listing points.
terms.do: Point, then a key moment, then what it shows.

terms.def: Using evidence from: key moments, quotes and details from the texts.
terms.do: Ground every point in a specific moment.

terms.def: The texts you studied for the comparative: for you, three of Sive, Othello, The Shawshank Redemption and Small Things Like These.
terms.do: Name them, with their authors or director, in your introduction.

terms.def: The quotation given at the start of the question.
terms.do: Agree, disagree, or partly agree with it, and say so early.

terms.def: The world of the text: who has power, what people value, and how they live: money, class, religion, family, men and women.
The text's outlook on life: is it bleak or hopeful, and how does that change from the opening to the ending?
A big idea the text explores, like power, love, freedom or identity, and what it says about it.

Being able to move up (or down) from one social position to another: from poor to rich, from a servant to a master, from nobody to somebody. Ask: can people in this world change where they stand, and what does it cost them?

eg.sive: Hardly any. A poor girl's only way up is a marriage for money: Mena married Mike to escape poverty, and Sive is to be married off to old Seán Dóta for his money.
eg.othello: Othello rose from slavery to general of Venice's army, yet Venice still treats him as an outsider. Iago is bitter that Cassio was promoted over him.
eg.shawshank: Inside, the only way up is being useful to the powerful: Andy goes from new arrival to the warden's banker. The only way out is parole or escape.
eg.stlt: Bill rose from the son of an unmarried servant girl to owner of the coal yard, thanks to Mrs Wilson's kindness. But his place depends on staying on the right side of the nuns.

terms.def: Where a person stands in their society: their rank, class or status, and how others treat them because of it.
A group of people with similar money, work and standing: for example, landowners, labourers, the poor.
A line that splits a society into groups: rich and poor, men and women, insiders and outsiders, the powerful and the powerless.
The world of people the text shows: its community, its rules, and who belongs where.
Your rank or importance in the eyes of others.
Who controls people and events, and how: through money, authority, violence or words.

eg.sive: Money and the matchmaker: Mena and Thomasheen arrange Sive's life for Seán Dóta's £200.
eg.othello: Venice's Senate and Othello's command on one side; Iago's power is all in his words.
eg.shawshank: Warden Norton and the guards: discipline, violence and the Bible.
eg.stlt: The Church: the nuns run the convent and the school, and the town keeps quiet.

terms.def: What people believe matters most: money, land, faith, family, reputation, love.
How people think and feel about something, and how that shows in what they do.
What a person holds to be true or right.
The unwritten rules of how people are expected to behave in that society.
On top: the most powerful or most common.
A society where men hold the power and women are expected to obey them.

eg.othello: Desdemona is treated as her father's property, then her husband's. Emilia's speech in the willow scene pushes back against it.
eg.sive: Sive has no say in her own marriage: it's arranged over her head for money. A woman has no name till she takes a husband, Mena tells her.

terms.def: Run by men, with men in the positions of power.
Going along with what everyone else expects, even when you disagree.
Someone stepping in to change what happens.
Something that sparks a change or makes it happen faster.
What people are really like, deep down: kind or cruel, brave or selfish.
What it's like to be human: love, loss, fear, hope, death.
Opposite or clashing: two things that can't both seem true at once.
Having many sides; not simple or black and white.
The strength to keep going and recover after hardship.

eg.shawshank: Andy: nearly twenty years of digging with a tiny rock hammer, and he never gives up hope.

terms.def: Being honest and sticking to what you believe is right, even when it costs you.
Feeling for other people's suffering and wanting to help.

eg.stlt: Bill can't stop thinking about the girls at the convent, and in the end he brings Sarah home.

terms.def: Being good to others, often in small, everyday ways.
Showing life as better or more perfect than it really is.
Showing life as it really is, warts and all.
True for people everywhere and at any time, not just in the world of the text.
Seeming to contradict itself but still true, like a prison that gives a man hope.
Given less of a chance than others; disempowered means having your power taken away.
Inclusive: letting everyone belong. Exclusive: shutting some people out.
About right and wrong.
Being different from what's normal or expected.
Put up with or allowed, even if not liked.
Being yourself, different from others; individual rights are what each person is entitled to.
A time of great trouble or danger, when things could go either way.
Where people share power and have a say in decisions.
A way of thinking that shapes how you see things.
To care for something and help it grow; instilled means put into someone's mind over time.
How you see and understand something.
The view or feeling you're left with.
A new or deeper understanding.
How a text looks closely at something and examines it from different sides.
How something or someone is shown.
Important: it changes something or tells us something.
Clear to see; shown.
Show or uncover something that wasn't clear before.
A part or side of something.
Something that causes or helps cause a result.
To affect or shape something. Over-influential means having too strong an effect.
To form something, or make it what it is.
A turning point: the moment everything changes.
The point of highest tension, where everything comes to a head.
Sorted out by the end, so we know how things stand.
A main character, the one the story is most about.
Connected to something, so it matters to it.
How a text makes you feel, and why.
Not allowed, or seen as wrong, in that society.
